newsitem.title: USA: A balanced-budget plan with tax cuts becomes law.
newsitem.headline: A balanced-budget plan with tax cuts becomes law.

text.p: Amid patriotic fanfare and predictions of cooperation with Congress, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday signed legislation aimed at balancing the U.S. budget and giving Americans $95 billion in tax cuts.
In stark contrast to the rancour that consumed past efforts to reach a budget, Republican Speaker Newt Gingrich stood with Clinton on a stage set up on the South Lawn to celebrate the legislation.

"We come here today, Democrats and Republicans, Congress and president, Americans of goodwill from all points of view and all walks of life, to celebrate a true milestone for our nation," Clinton said.
"This has been a long time coming," said Gingrich. "It has been a difficult process. But in that process we have proven together that the American constitutional system works."

Clinton signed two bills, approved last week by the Republican-controlled Congress, one that aims to balance the budget by the year 2002 and a companion piece that cuts taxes by a net $95 billion over five years.
Under the line-item budget authority that went into effect this year, Clinton still has until Monday to veto any of 79 tax breaks aimed at specific companies or individuals.
White House officials said a review of the massive legislation was still under way and that it was not clear whether Clinton would use his authority.

House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt, who opposed the budget deal and did not attend the ceremony, urged Clinton to veto a provision that would let the tobacco industry credit a new tax against any eventual nationwide settlement it makes.

The package includes a 10 cent increase on cigarette packs in 2000, rising an additional five cents in 2002. The tax hike would be credited against any tobacco settlement between the industry and 40 states.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton could not follow Gephardt's request. "I don't think the line item veto is available in the case of that particular item," he said.

Despite the lavish praise used during the lengthy ceremony held under sunny skies, critics and the public remained sceptical the legislation will end the deficit that has plagued federal spending for so long.

Clinton and Gingrich, however, spoke only of the historic nature of the agreement and the bright hopes that it raises for future legislation -- in effect burying the bickering of the past that twice shut down the federal government.
"I hope we can tap this spirit of cooperation and use it to meet and master the many challenges that remain before us," Clinton said.

Gingrich, caught up in the euphoria, not only declared "we have a chance to work together to accomplish a lot," but pledged to work with Clinton and Democrats in Congress to "make bipartisan progress at home, and...provide bipartisan leadership across the planet."
The budget legislation reduces Medicare and Medicaid spending, creates a new children's health programme and restores some spending cuts in last year's welfare law.
The tax bill includes a $500 per child credit, a reduction in the capital gains rate and new tax incentives for higher education.

"On the whole, it is disappointing," said Robert Greenstein, an analyst with the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities, of the budget deal. He said "this bill balances the budget in the short-term, rather than in the long-term."

A poll for Time Magazine and CNN released over the weekend found that 62 percent believed it was "somewhat or very unlikely" that the legislation will produce a balanced budget by the year 2002, while only 27 percent said the tax cuts would be "fair" to all Americans.
